articles.title: LS Lowry review – matchstick men, or the broken denizens of a smog-filled hellscape?
articles.text:
While people queue at the British Museum to see the Battle of Hastings, this excellent survey of LS Lowry at the MK Gallery in Milton Keynes takes you back to another, maybe more decisive part of our past – the age when Britain was the most industrialised society on Earth. Laurence Lowry was born in 1887 and worked for 41 years as a rent collector, a job that took him all over his native Greater Manchester observing its people and places. He had the city’s grime and grind in his soul. The MK wants to show him as a fully rounded artist, to uncover the Lowry with a song in his heart, but it’s the misery of his urban hell that holds and harrows you.

In his 1930 painting Coming from the Mill it’s the end of the shift and scores of people emerge from a factory’s bleak yellow gatehouse as if leaving prison. Their daily captivity has left them broken and exhausted and the little abstracted figures hunch forwards as they walk without pausing to laugh or chat, going to their separate homes, each one withdrawn, wretched. They are not the painting’s protagonists – they are passive victims. The architecture of industry dominates the picture as it rules their lives. How can any of these little people, dwarfed by the mill that eats their time and energy, attain individuality? No wonder they all look the same except for minor variations in their drab clothes. They’ve been reduced by the Industrial Revolution to matchstick people.

Lowry is the Franz Kafka of industrial Britain. He is not a naive artist who painted crudely because that’s the best he could do. Nor is he a patient social realist laying bare the injustices of capitalism – although Friedrich Engels would surely have recognised his Manchester. He is a modern expressionist who finds his inner melancholy reflected in the industrial sublime. He drinks in its despair, feasts on its poetry of alienation. As you journey through Lowry’s North, you sink ever further into his personal slough of despond.

Slough of Despond would make a good alternative title for his 1924 drawing The River Irwell at the Adelphi. Heaps of mud and ash choke the slow-moving river that runs through Salford, its shores lined with decaying sheds and slums against a smoggy, chimney-lined sky. It’s Lowry at his purest as he depicts the stunning, crushing presence of the city itself. He draws and paints the black, gnarled spires of urban churches with as much relish as those monstrous mills. In the second world war he was a fire-watcher with a privileged view of the blitz: a drawing of freshly bombed buildings in Piccadilly, Manchester shows husks of charred brick still wreathed in smoke.

This show digs out other, less well known dimensions to his talent. But his paintings of the Lake District are even more chilling than his cities. Lake Landscape, painted in 1950, is a vista of low curving hills divided by silvery still water, receding in abstract, musical pulses of sadness. No people or animals inhabit this eerie world. When he paints people close up it’s even more disturbing: a young man with staring eyes, a father and sons who all seem equally desperate. He lightens up to paint his ideal woman with a simplified doll-like face apparently intended as his tribute to Pre-Raphaelite red-lipped beauties but the result is weirdly robotic. Her face is on the exhibition merchandise, perhaps because Halloween is coming.

The most bizarre painting, however, is his 1963 work In a Park. At first glance it’s another city crowd scene until you realise everyone in this fenced enclosure has something different about them. A one-eyed face screams while people walk around the white-earthed, empty space with spinal deformities, facial palsies, amputated limbs. The catalogue gets itself in knots – is Lowry mocking the disabled or questioning how we define disability?

But this painting is not about disability in a political sense at all. It uses it as an image of humanity in general: all people are broken and alone, misshapen in Lowry’s hopeless universe.

Lowry is a tricky customer. If it is pure snobbery to look down on him for being popular it is also patronising to see this troubled artist as a warmly sentimental nostalgist of the north. He is a painter of modern life in the age when that meant huge crowds staggering home in the shadow of smoking chimneys in cities blackened by carbon. At his best, Lowry is a great modern artist. His 1919 painting Pit Tragedy shows working-class people waiting for the worst news. They are statuesque, tragically posed in the grey dusty light. A woman turns towards us, her head veiled. Her pain is lost in the past but lives on here, observed and recorded by Lowry, visionary of the industrial age.

articles.title: ‘I laughed so hard my Tampax fell out’: Michael Gambon’s pranks revealed by the stars he cracked up
articles.text:
Jasper Rees’s authorised biography of Michael Gambon, published three years after the great actor’s death, has nuanced accounts of his performances in Shakespeare, Beckett and Pinter as well as The Singing Detective and the Harry Potter films. There are even chapters devoted to his hands (“the biggest you’ve ever seen on anybody” – Brian Cox) and similarly enormous feet. But, Gambon being Gambon, there are also dozens of accounts of tomfoolery on and off stage …

‘One of the funniest people I’ve ever met’

David Hare’s 1995 play Skylight is set in a draughty flat where a dish of spaghetti is cooked up on stage. Those kitchen cupboards proved useful for Lia Williams to hide when Gambon’s goofing got to her at the National Theatre. Gambon would adopt a different accent or speak in tongues during a scene and “when he made me laugh it was hell on Earth because there was nothing I could do about it” said Williams, who called him “one of the funniest people I’ve ever met”. She continued: “One time I laughed so hard that my Tampax fell out and I had to deal with that for an entire act.”

Dinner with Judi, Ken and Natasha

Ibsen’s Ghosts was a hot potato when it was first staged in 1882 thanks to its scandalous plot involving syphilis and incest. Gambon had some fun with the spuds when playing the self-righteous Pastor Manders in an 80s BBC TV version. Director Elijah Moshinsky envisioned a tense, sombre dinner scene and Gambon sat alongside Judi Dench and Kenneth Branagh. The potatoes were duly passed around by Natasha Richardson. “I’ll just have the usual eight,” requested Gambon. His co-stars’ corpsing led them to leave the set. “We couldn’t control ourselves at all,” confessed Dench.

Dumbledore unleashes Fartis Temporus

Not every actor’s biography includes “fart machines” in the index but toots fake and real are let off in several chapters. When Gambon took over the role of Dumbledore in Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, he and Alan Rickman pranked Daniel Radcliffe by triggering a fart machine during a closeup of the young star when he was in a sleeping bag alongside fellow Hogwarts students. “I was initially really annoyed,” said Radcliffe, before concluding that if Rickman and Gambon had engineered it then “that is pretty funny”.

A storm and a Fool

When Gambon played King Lear for the RSC in 1982, Antony Sher sported a red nose as the clownish Fool. The poster presented them as a sort of double act and Sher was widely seen as stealing the limelight. Rees likens it to Gambon taking on what is often referred to as an “actor’s Everest” only to find another climber “clambering frantically up the same rope”. Adrian Noble, who directed the tragedy, said Gambon “joshed [Sher] mercilessly”. During the storm scene he reportedly bellowed: “Come on out, you little red-nosed fucker!”

When he was appearing on stage in Arthur Miller’s A View from the Bridge, Gambon kept a signed photo of Robert De Niro – with words of admiration for Gambon’s work – on his dressing room table. The pair would appear together in the film The Good Shepherd in 2006 but had never even met by the time he was doing A View from the Bridge. The fake autograph and note – “I loved working with you Mike, you’re great – love Bobby” – were apparently written by Gambon himself.

One festive season in the late 60s, Gambon found himself starring in the Christmas show Hans, the Witch and the Gobbin at Birmingham Rep – much to his annoyance, remembered co-star Anthony Higgins. A prodigious swearer, Gambon decided to add to his stage makeup for a performance. “One night he’d written on one eyelid ‘fuck’ and on the other ‘off’,” said Higgins. Gambon blinked each eye to deliver the message to Higgins. Artistic director Peter Dews had to give him a word of warning.

‘Rupert wet himself regularly’

When Gambon played the tramp Davies in a 2000 revival of Harold Pinter’s play The Caretaker, he revelled in repelling theatregoers – as well as the brothers played by Douglas Hodge and Rupert Graves. One night, according to Rees’s book, Gambon had his back to the audience and buried his hand in his trousers, where he had stowed away a serving of chocolate cake. He withdrew his smeared fingers and sniffed them, causing his co-stars to crack up. “Rupert was in terrible trouble,” remembered Hodge. “Rupert wet himself regularly.”

A fry-up with Cleopatra

Gambon loved to supply journalists with tall tales and see who believed him. He treated one interviewer to an “insight” into how he and Helen Mirren prepared while in the wings for their roles as Antony and Cleopatra for the RSC. Mirren, he assured the journalist, got into character by performing a mime in which she prepared a dish of ham and eggs for Antony. “Absolute rubbish,” Mirren told Rees, though added: “It’s a lovely story.”
